content: I’m calling it: time of death, November 6th, 1:30 AM, by tweet. Elon Musk’s declaration Friday that Tesla would be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck next year to make room for the Cybercab was fascinating for a number of reasons. First, it was a humiliating way to kill a vehicle that was once hailed as the pinnacle of Tesla’s engineering — faster than a Porsche 911, more powerful than an F-150, able to leap over the Model Y as a singular representation of Musk’s Blade Runner-inspired designs for the future. “I think the Tesla Cybertruck is our best product ever,” he declared during a 2019 earnings call. (He prefaced the statement by saying, “This could be totally wrong. I could be totally out to lunch here.” It would appear so!) The fact that Musk would just quietly put an end to the Cybertruck without any fanfare was a sign of how far it had fallen, not just in the eyes of the public, but in the eyes of its creator, the man most responsible for brute-forcing this low-emission, low-poly technological nightmare into the world. Tesla actually thought the Cybertruck would be a huge hit, targeting production and demand of 250,000 units per year. To date, the company has only sold 70,000 units — total. Musk’s other company, SpaceX, ended up being one of the largest single purchasers of Cybertrucks to absorb unsold inventory. Musk had to become his own customer to make the Cybertruck look better on paper. But the death of the Cybertruck is even more noteworthy given the timing of Musk’s tweet, coming just three days after his epic flop at the ballot box. Musk poured over $445 million into Republican races, with most of his money targeting his home turf of Texas — headquarters to both Tesla and SpaceX. Between funnels of $168 million to super PACs backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton and nearly $35 million redirected from his own America PAC, Musk dropped more than $200 million on the Lone Star State alone. All that money, and zero return. Democrat James Talarico crushed Paxton by 12 points to break a 38-year Democratic Senate drought, while Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion. Texas turned blue, despite the best efforts of the world’s richest man — or perhaps because of them? Americans are fed up: they don’t want Musk meddling in their government, and they especially don’t want his stainless-steel monument to his own vanity and utter refusal to accept human feedback. The Cybertruck was one of the most epic failures in modern automotive history. While it succeeded as a viral PR spectacle and initially became a top-selling premium electric pickup in early 2024, it ultimately collapsed under the weight of Musk’s own hubris. The reasons for the Cybertruck’s failures are almost too many to enumerate: too expensive, not as much range or towing power as promised, too many recalls, and, well, it looked the way it did. But when Musk outed himself as a Trump supporter, forever tying himself to Trump’s MAGA brand, the Cybertruck went with him. Electric vehicles are typically associated with a style of coastal progressivism, but the Cybertruck crossed the aisle to become a physical avatar of Trump’s ugly brand of politics. And more so than any other car in modern history, the Cybertruck was inseparable from its creator. By the time Musk threw hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s campaign, launched the America PAC, and took a prominent position in Trump’s administration as the head of the disastrous DOGE project, owning a Cybertruck had become a rolling liability. People who owned a Model 3 or Model Y could credibly claim they bought it before “Elon went crazy,” as the bumper stickers would later declare — a Cybertruck owner could make no such claim. To be sure, most people who bought Cybertrucks were not interested in distancing themselves from Musk’s brand of trollish politics. A big part of MAGA culture is owning the libs. And because liberals, car purists, and environmentalists couldn’t stand the Cybertruck — mocking everything from its sharp edges to its build quality — buying one became a way to get under their skin. Before long, people were slapping Trump wraps on them, flying flags from the truck beds, and turning them into props for conservative rallies. But vibes shift, as they always do. Edgelords lose their edge, and voters become weary and wary of efforts to divide them. The blue tsunami was a historic rejection of Trump and Musk’s brand of right-wing grievance politics. When the spectacle wore off, the bluster stopped feeling like rebellion and started looking like a shit way to run a government. In a single election, the country said it was done. The results on Tuesday also rendered the Cybertruck an instant relic. The election stripped away the sheen of inevitability that once insulated both the billionaire and his pet project. It’s a relief, but a peculiar one at that. Has there ever been a vehicle so desperate to look like the future, only to become an immediate symbol of the past?

chineseContent: 我在推特上称其为：死亡时间，11 月 6 日凌晨 1:30。埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 周五宣布，特斯拉将在明年“停止” Cyber​​truck 的生产，为 Cyber​​cab 腾出空间，这一声明令人着迷，原因有很多。首先，这是一种羞辱性的方式来扼杀一辆曾经被誉为特斯拉工程巅峰的汽车——比保时捷 911 更快，比 F-150 更强大，能够超越 Model Y，成为马斯克受《银翼杀手》启发的未来设计的独特代表。 “我认为 Tesla Cyber​​truck 是我们有史以来最好的产品，”他在 2019 年财报电话会议上宣称。 （他在声明的前言中说，“这可能是完全错误的。我完全可以在这里吃午饭。”看来是这样！）事实上，马斯克悄无声息地结束了赛博卡车，这一事实表明它已经堕落到了何种程度，不仅在公众眼中，而且在它的创造者眼中，这个人对这个低排放、低聚合的技术噩梦负有最大责任。特斯拉实际上认为 Cyber​​truck 会大受欢迎，目标是每年 25 万辆的产量和需求。迄今为止，该公司总共只售出了 70,000 台。马斯克的另一家公司 SpaceX 最终成为吸收未售出库存的 Cyber​​truck 最大单一买家之一。马斯克必须成为自己的客户，才能让 Cyber​​truck 在纸面上看起来更好。但考虑到马斯克发推文的时机，赛博卡车的死亡更值得注意，就在他在投票箱中惨败的三天后。马斯克向共和党竞选投入了超过 4.45 亿美元，其中大部分资金都投向了他的家乡德克萨斯州——特斯拉和 SpaceX 的总部。向支持共和党的超级政治行动委员会提供 1.68 亿美元
